claim: A main weakness of novices in program execution is a non-viable model of the machine, not syntax; about one third hold non-viable models of value assignment and most hold non-viable models of object reference, and wrong models cluster on a few types.
agent_test: Check whether the agent, on small programs with aliasing and assignment, makes the same clustered errors when it traces without a table.

claim: Explicit written step-by-step tracing (doodles, tracing tables, scratchpads) goes with higher correctness than none, in students and in language models.
agent_test: Compare plain answer vs forced state-table trace on a code-output set at equal tokens.

claim: In students the benefit of tracing is conditional on form: synchronized trace about 77% correct, blank page 50%, loose number jotting about 70%, computation 60%.
agent_test: Test free-form trace vs structured per-line state table on the agent.

claim: Teaching an explicit tracing strategy to novices raised tracing scores (d about 0.72, N=24, p=.049), largest on many-variable programs; sample tiny and p borderline.
agent_test: Strategy prompt vs none on many-variable programs.

claim: Teaching the machine directly (PLTutor) gave 60% higher learning gain than Codecademy in a 4.3 hour study, but N=18 vs 19 after data loss. An independent tutor study (N=48) with and without an explicit notional machine found no difference (d14); no study with N above 100 found.
agent_test: Analogue: give the agent a written machine-rule sheet in the prompt (see K08).

claim: Visualisation plus cognitive conflict repaired wrong assignment models better than visualisation alone (90% vs 62.5%, N=18), and failed to repair half of wrong execution-flow models.
agent_test: Show the agent its prediction next to the real output (conflict) vs a rule restatement; compare fix rate.

claim: The claim that a consistent mental model predicts programming success (camel has two humps) was retracted by its author; consistency as an aptitude signal is not established.
agent_test: No test; do not treat self-consistency of the agent's stated rules as correctness.

claim: Learners infer their own, often over-restrictive rules of program behaviour; explicit rule sets are proposed as a fix but have no learner experiment.
agent_test: Give the agent an explicit semantics ruleset vs none; compare trace accuracy on edge semantics.

claim: The term notional machine is used loosely: about half of 226 papers define it and 27% use one in an intervention; causal evidence that notional-machine teaching beats alternatives is thin.
agent_test: None; a warning about the evidence base.

claim: Without CoT, LLMs predict output of short functions poorly (GPT-4 63% output on CRUXEval, best open 44%); newer reasoning models do far better.
agent_test: Run the agent's code-run step vs in-head prediction on the same functions; the gap is the value of S2 execution.

claim: CoT tracing helps strong models on output prediction (GPT-4 63 to 81.9%) but can hurt weak ones, which lose items solved directly.
agent_test: Per-model gate: use trace prompts only after a pilot shows gain; otherwise run real code.

claim: Model-written traces help debugging little or not at all: +1.8 points over explanation on MBPP, CoT cut untuned code models by 7.8 points on HumanEvalFix-Plus, GPT-3.5 gets no lift from traces.
agent_test: Prefer real execution traces over model-written ones when revising.

claim: Real execution traces as input improve repair after trace-aware training (PaLM 2-L +26.1 on Mbpp-R) and for GPT-4 but not GPT-3.5. Gap search: symptoms-only vs real runtime trace ablation lost 26.3% of fixes on GPT-3.5/Defects4J (d05); still no equal-token test on untuned frontier models.
agent_test: Feed the actual trace of the failing run into the revision slot vs the error message only.

claim: Model-written execution reasoning is often unfaithful: 81% of simulations were coherent but only 47% of those were correct; only about 30% of rationales explained the error correctly.
agent_test: Never accept a stated trace as evidence; compare against code-run.

claim: Success on code-output prediction is not understanding: under perturbation accuracy drops up to about 54 points for non-reasoning coders and 19.5 for GPT-5.2, while reasoning models are stable.
agent_test: Evaluate the agent's trace on a mutated input of the same program.

claim: Code reasoning is not code generation or repair skill: distilled models gain on HumanEval but not CRUXEval; repair does not correlate with reasoning except at the frontier; 39-45% of successful repairs were shortcuts.
agent_test: Do not infer correct code from good trace skill; check by running.

claim: Reasoning accuracy falls with program complexity (nesting, loops, non-primitive types, length); errors are mostly computation then control flow.
agent_test: Allocate execution budget by complexity; for long loops use code-run, not simulation.

claim: One ground-truth input/output example in the prompt raises code-synthesis pass@1 by 5.36 points on average (9.78 ClassEval, 0.94 HumanEval).
agent_test: Give the agent one concrete worked I/O example at S2 vs none.

claim: Tool-augmented tracing fixes many simulation errors: 58% of sampled computation errors corrected; Chain of Code gained 12 points on BIG-Bench Hard over CoT.
agent_test: Compare in-head simulation vs code interpreter at equal tokens.

claim: Fine-tuning on execution traces raises trace skill sharply (Llama3.1 8B full-state 10.6% prompted to 96.3% fine-tuned; CWM 94.3% CruxEval-O) but is training, outside our scaffold.
agent_test: Out of scope; an upper bound on what a scaffold might recover.

claim: LLMs identify and simulate novice misconceptions well on multiple choice, but fabricate problems in student explanations (27% on fully correct input).
agent_test: Use an LLM misconception check only on flagged cases because false alarms are frequent.

claim: LLMs answer questions about programs well (GPT-4 88%) but invent justifications for wrong answers; GPT-4 traces visual programs far better than GPT-3.5 (60 vs 10).
agent_test: Do not trust the explanation that comes with an answer.

claim: Human working memory limits explain tracing errors; substitution errors are 70% more common than calculation errors (link to the working-memory subfield).
agent_test: Test whether an externalised state table cuts variable-lookup errors in the agent.

claim: Many novices fail simple tracing questions in large multi-country samples (bottom quartile 0-4 of 12; over 60% wrong on execution questions in cited studies); fragile skills outnumber misconceptions.
agent_test: Human baseline context; no direct agent test.

claim: Telling the model something about language behaviour in the prompt can move accuracy more than the model choice, but the same rule can over-trigger: one sentence about exceptions took GPT-5.2 from 15% to 81% on exception cases, yet cost about 5 points on ordinary cases. A full semantics rule sheet has not been tested.
agent_test: Rule sheet vs plain CoT on edge-case programs at equal tokens; score ordinary cases too, to catch over-triggering.

claim: Feedback from the real interpreter helps revision; the model's own review without it gives little or nothing, and can hurt. In reasoning tasks without an outside signal, self-correction lowers accuracy (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0).
agent_test: Feed true run output next to the agent's wrong prediction; do not let the agent judge its own trace.

claim: Chain of thought helps mostly where steps are execution (computation, tracing); a tool that runs the steps beats model-written steps. Meta-analysis of 110 papers: +14.2 symbolic, +12.3 math, +6.9 logic points; other tasks 56.8 vs 56.1.
agent_test: Route pure execution (long loops, arithmetic) to code-run; keep model-written trace for planning and short programs.

claim: Revision on the model's own feedback pays off only for strong models and bigger budgets; at equal tokens weak models do as well or better by resampling. No tested per-task detector of the crossover exists.
agent_test: Pilot gate: equal-token resample vs revise on a handful of items.

claim: LLM errors on reference, aliasing and mutation semantics have not been measured. Error taxonomies of reasoning models list computation first and contain no aliasing category; weak benchmarks rarely stress it.
agent_test: Build a small alias and mutation probe set (shared list, copy vs reference, in-place vs new object) and compare with value-assignment items.
